articles.title: Tarifaço: Brasil espera proposta de acordo esta semana ou a próxima | G1
articles.standfirst: Oferta pode levar a um acordo entre os países. Documento deverá trazer sugestões de concessões comerciais, como reduções tarifárias em determinados setores, por exemplo.
articles.summary: O ministro Márcio Elias Rosa afirmou que o Brasil aguarda uma proposta dos EUA com reduções de impostos para resolver o impasse do tarifaço ainda esta semana.
articles.body:
O ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC), Márcio Elias Rosa, afirmou que o Brasil deve receber entre esta semana e o início da próxima uma oferta de eventual acordo por parte dos Estados Unidos sobre o tarifaço.

O documento deverá trazer sugestões de concessões comerciais, como reduções tarifárias em determinados setores, por exemplo.

"Nós tivemos uma reunião nos Estados Unidos em 30 de setembro, e eles ficaram de encaminhar um termo de referência, que é o nome que usamos para um esboço do que pode ser um futuro acordo, em três ou quatro semanas. Essa é a quarta semana. Então, imagino que o Brasil deva receber esse documento entre esta semana e a próxima", disse o ministro a jornalistas.

Elias Rosa explicou que, em negociações comerciais desse tipo, uma das partes apresenta uma proposta inicial, à qual a outra responde com suas ofertas e contrapropostas.

"Quando negociamos um acordo dessa natureza, uma parte apresenta uma proposta e nós fazemos as nossas ofertas. Eles devem nos encaminhar um documento indicando, basicamente, quais são os setores em que gostariam de obter reduções tarifárias, por exemplo, e nós responderemos em seguida. Mas ainda não houve nenhuma antecipação sobre o mérito da proposta", declarou Elias.

Segundo Elias Rosa, o governo americano está trabalhando na elaboração do texto . "A informação que eu tenho é que eles estão preparando o documento para nos encaminhar. Independentemente da discussão política, nós mantivemos conversas informais nesse período, e eles de fato estão trabalhando nisso", afirmou.

"Eles fazem uma proposta dos setores que a eles interessa, e nós vamos responder de acordo com aquilo que convém ao Brasil", completou.

Ao ser questionado se as eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos , as chamadas mditerms, poderiam ter alguma influência na negociação sobre o tarifaço, o ministro foi categórico: "Não, nada. Não muda absolutamente nada".

"O Brasil segue o seu percurso, seu trabalho, temos muito trabalho a fazer, e é o povo americano que define as eleições", complementou.

Ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Elias Rosa, durante o programa “Bom Dia, Ministro”, na EBC — Foto: Júlio César Silva/MDIC

O Brasil foi alvo de rodadas de tarifaços anunciadas pelo governo dos EUA:

de 25% : em razão do entendimento da Casa Branca de que o Brasil adota práticas desleais na economia em relação a empresários americanos em áreas como PIX, etanol e propriedade intelectual;

de 12,5% : diante do entendimento dos EUA de que dezenas de países, incluindo o Brasil, falharam ao coibir a importação de mercadorias de países onde há trabalho forçado.

🎤 Durante as negociações para tentar evitar o tarifaço, representantes do governo brasileiro disseram que os americanos desconsideraram os argumentos técnicos, o que levou o Brasil a considerar que as medidas tiveram caráter político, não comercial.

Nesse contexto, o Brasil abriu um pedido de consultas na Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC), alegando que ao agir dessa maneira os EUA tratam o Brasil de maneira diferente dos demais parceiros comerciais.

Em resposta, os Estados Unidos informaram à OMC estarem à disposição do Brasil para discutir o tema, mas ainda não indicaram, segundo diplomatas brasileiros, qualquer sinal de reversão do tarifaço.

Em setembro, representantes dos presidentes Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Donald Trump se reuniram em Genebra, na sede da OMC, para negociar.

Com isso, abriu-se o prazo de 60 dias para que os dois países cheguem a um consenso. Se não houver acordo no prazo, uma das partes pode abrir um painel, ou seja, pedir que o tema vá a julgamento pela OMC.

O governo da China pediu formalmente à OMC para participar do processo, mas os EUA se manifestaram contra a abertura de espaço para os chineses.

Após uma longa discussão, o presidente Lula sancionou, em setembro, a Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos , que estabelece diretrizes para as etapas de pesquisa, lavra, beneficiamento, transformação mineral e mineração urbana.

Além disso, foi instalado o Conselho para o setor, que deve fazer a primeira reunião do pleno logo após agendas internacionais do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nas próximas semanas.

Na ocasião, deve ser discutida a lista de minerais que serão classificados como críticos e estratégicos. Sobre o assunto, o ministro disse nesta terça-feira (3) que não deverá ter surpresa.

"A definição inicial da lista, aquela lista rotativa do que seja minerais críticos, do que seja estratégicos a definição da lista, não tem muito segredo, todo mundo que é especialista no tema sabe, pode eventualmente se surpreender com a ausência de algum, mas também não tem ministério", disse.

A política considera como críticos os minerais cujo abastecimento está sujeito a riscos capazes de afetar setores essenciais da economia.

Já os estratégicos são aqueles considerados importantes para o desenvolvimento tecnológico e regional, para a balança comercial ou para a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa.

🔍O Brasil ainda não tem uma lista oficial de minerais classificados como críticos e estratégicos.

Esses minerais têm aplicações em áreas diversas, como transição energética, digitalização, defesa e indústria de alta tecnologia.

Lítio, níquel, cobalto, grafita e manganês são usados em baterias de íon-lítio, por exemplo. Os veículos elétricos, por sua vez, também utilizam minerais como lítio, cobre e níquel, além de terras raras, em sua composição.

"Deveremos ter a lista dos minerais críticos, uma diretriz para um plano nacional, que é como a lei chama, e nós teremos depois uma discussão um pouco mais demorada que é triagem dos investimentos", explicou Elias, acrescentando que essa etapa pode ocorrer em um segundo momento, porque primeiro deve ser definido as cadeias produtivas prioritárias.

"E aí eu aproveito para dizer: no momento que o governo definir as cadeias prioritárias, ele não excluirá outras. A exemplo da lista elas também são determinadas pela demanda. Baterias constituem uma prioridade, não significa que não poderá ser agregada a outras. É só um ponto de partida", explicou.

articles.title: Lula embarca para São Paulo, onde vai fazer exames de rotina nesta ter | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente retorna a Brasília na manhã de quarta-feira (4), segundo a Secretaria de Comunicação do Palácio do Planalto. Exames já estavam pré-agendados para depois da eleição.
articles.summary: Presidente retorna a Brasília na manhã de quarta-feira (4), segundo a Secretaria de Comunicação do Palácio do Planalto. Exames já estavam pré-agendados para depois da eleição.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) embarcou para São Paulo na tarde desta terça-feira (3) para realizar exames de rotina no Hospital Sírio-Libanês.

Segundo a Secretaria de Comunicação (Secom) da Presidência da República, os exames já estavam pré-agendados para depois da eleição. Lula está com 81 anos.

Os exames serão realizados ainda nesta terça, sob coordenação do cardiologista Roberto Kalil Filho e da médica Ana Helena Germoglio.

A previsão é que Lula retorne a Brasília na manhã desta quarta (4) e siga normalmente com a agenda de trabalho ( leia mais abaixo ).

Em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais nesta segunda (1º), o presidente afirmou que ficou a semana passada sem voz e que "fez muito" para se recuperar.

No vídeo, ele reclamava da disseminação de notícias falsas relacionadas aos programas sociais do governo.

"Numa semana que fiquei sem falar, a mentira tomou conta desse país outra vez. A extrema-direita fez muita fake news dizendo que nós íamos acabar com programas sociais. Escuta o que vou dizer para vocês: nenhum programa social será extinto neste país", afirmou na ocasião.

Questionada, a equipe médica do presidente negou que a visita ao hospital não tenha relação com a rouquidão do presidente .

Na ocasião, o hospital informou que todos os exames estavam dentro da normalidade. A equipe responsável pelo acompanhamento também era liderada por Roberto Kalil Filho e Ana Helena Germoglio.

Em maio, Lula voltou ao hospital para acompanhar a evolução de procedimentos realizados em abril. Segundo boletim divulgado na ocasião, o presidente apresentava "evolução satisfatória" e mantinha suas atividades habituais.

articles.title: When will Texas election results be available? What to know Election Day
articles.summary: Texas polls close at 7 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3. Here's when election results are expected and why some races could take longer to call.
articles.body:
Texans will get their first look at the 2026 midterm election results after polls close, but some races may take hours or more to decide.

Polls across Texas close at 7 p.m. local time Tuesday, Nov. 3. Preliminary results are expected to begin appearing shortly afterward, with the first reported totals generally reflecting ballots cast during early voting and mail-in voting.

The Texas Secretary of State's Office said statewide and district-level results may begin appearing in its Election Night Returns system around 7:30 p.m. Counties also report results through their own election websites.

When do Texas polls close on Election Day?

Texas polling locations close at 7 p.m. local time Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Most of the state observes Central Time, but El Paso and Hudspeth counties are in the Mountain Time Zone. Polls in those counties close at 7 p.m. Mountain Time.

Voters in line when polls close can still cast a ballot. That means some polling locations may not begin reporting Election Day results until later in the evening.

When will Texas election results start coming in?

The first unofficial results are expected shortly after 7 p.m. Central Time, and the state's reporting system may begin populating around 7:30 p.m.

Counties typically report early voting and mail-in ballot totals first. Election Day results follow as ballots are transported from polling locations to county election offices and counting stations.

Results will continue to be updated throughout the night and into Wednesday, Nov. 4, as counties finish counting and reporting ballots.

The Texas Secretary of State's Office does not call races or declare winners. It provides election results reported by counties.

Why could some Texas election results take longer?

Several factors can affect how quickly election results become available.

Election Day ballots: Unlike early voting totals, Election Day ballots cannot be counted until polls close. Ballots and voting equipment must also be transported to central counting locations.

Large counties: Counties with numerous polling locations may need more time to collect ballots and report totals.

Voters still in line: Anyone in line at 7 p.m. can still vote, which may delay reporting at some locations.

Mail and provisional ballots: Some eligible mail-in ballots, military and overseas ballots, and provisional ballots may be counted after Election Day.

Texas law generally requires counties to submit Election Day vote totals to the state within 24 hours after polls close.

Scenes of democracy unfold as Americans cast ballots on Election Day

When will Texas election results become official?

Election Night results are unofficial. County election officials must complete additional procedures, including canvassing and certification, before the state makes results official.

Eligible mail ballots postmarked by Election Day may arrive after polls close. Provisional ballots also require additional review, and eligible military and overseas ballots may arrive after Election Day.

The certification process takes place after election officials have completed the required counting and verification procedures.

That means a candidate or news organization declaring a winner on Election Night is not the same as the state officially certifying the results.

Where can I find Texas election results?

The Texas Secretary of State's Office will publish statewide and district-level election results through its Election Night Returns portal .

For local races and ballot measures, voters should check their county election office's website. County results may appear before the same totals are reflected in the statewide reporting system.

Who declares the winner of a Texas election?

The Texas Secretary of State's Office does not independently call races or declare winners on Election Night. Instead, it collects and publishes unofficial results reported by counties.

News organizations, including the USA TODAY Network, may project a winner once enough votes have been counted to determine the likely outcome. Campaigns also may concede or declare victory. Neither action makes the results official.

The official process involves election officials reviewing and canvassing the results before the appropriate authority certifies the outcome and issues a certificate of election.

In Texas, the process varies depending on the office:

County and precinct races: The local canvassing authority conducts the final canvass.

Statewide, federal and district races: The state canvass is the final canvass. The Secretary of State tabulates county returns, and the governor generally issues certificates of election.

Governor and lieutenant governor: The Texas House speaker handles their election certificates after the next Legislature convenes.

Can mail-in ballots arrive after Election Day?

Yes. Texas allows certain mail-in ballots to arrive after Election Day and still be counted, provided they meet specific deadlines and requirements.

Domestic mail ballots: Certain ballots from voters using a regular application for a ballot by mail may arrive by 5 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 4, if they are postmarked or otherwise marked by an approved carrier by 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Military and overseas ballots: Eligible military and overseas voters have additional time to return their ballots. The deadline for these ballots is Monday, Nov. 9.

Defective mail ballot envelopes: Voters whose carrier envelopes have certain correctable defects may have until Nov. 9 to correct them.

The Early Voting Ballot Board reviews these ballots and determines whether they meet the requirements to be counted. Not every ballot arriving after Election Day qualifies.

The board must finish counting eligible late-arriving ballots and resolving provisional ballots before the final canvass can take place.

A provisional ballot lets someone vote when election officials cannot immediately verify their eligibility.

This can happen if a voter's name does not appear on the registration list, their identification cannot be verified or they are attempting to vote in the wrong precinct, among other circumstances.

Provisional ballots are kept separate from regular ballots while election officials review the voter's eligibility.

County voter registrars investigate the voter's registration status and inform the Early Voting Ballot Board. The board, which includes members of both political parties, ultimately decides whether to count each provisional ballot.

Some voters who cast provisional ballots because of identification issues must take an additional step. They have until the sixth day after Election Day, Nov. 9, to present an acceptable form of identification or submit an applicable affidavit to their county voter registrar.

Not every provisional ballot is automatically counted. The board must determine that the voter was eligible and had not already voted in the election.

Voters will receive written notice explaining whether the board counted their provisional ballot. If it was rejected, the notice must include the reason.

What is canvassing, and when will Texas certify election results?

Canvassing is the formal process election officials use to review and reconcile election returns before certifying results.

During the process, officials verify vote totals and reconcile the number of ballots cast with the number of voters. They also account for eligible mail-in and provisional ballots that were not included in Election Night totals.

The canvass is not a recount. It is a required review of the election returns to establish the official results.

Texas has different canvassing deadlines depending on the office being contested.

Local, county and precinct races: The final local canvass must take place between Nov. 6 and Nov. 17, 2026.

Statewide, federal and district races: The final state canvass must take place between Nov. 21 and Dec. 7, 2026.

The state canvass occurs after counties complete their required reporting. The Secretary of State tabulates the returns, and the appropriate state authority issues the certificate of election.

That means the final, certified results for some of Texas' most closely watched races may not be available until weeks after Election Day.

For voters following the results Tuesday night, the important distinction is that Election Night totals are preliminary. A projected winner is not the same as a certified winner.

articles.title: FBI nabs suspect accused of sending hundreds of white powder letters to public officials: source
articles.summary: Federal investigators linked more than 700 suspicious mailings to the same sender, with fingerprints and surveillance footage allegedly tying the Oklahoma City suspect to the letters.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The FBI arrested an Oklahoma City man early Monday suspected of sending hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder to public officials across the country during the 2024 and 2026 election cycles, a federal law enforcement source told Fox News Digital. Robin Patrick Martin is charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications, according to a federal criminal complaint filed in the Western District of Oklahoma. Federal investigators linked more than 700 suspicious mailings sent in 2026 to the same sender, according to the complaint. The letters were addressed to state election boards, Republican, Democratic and independent members of Congress, pollsters, media organizations and the FBI. The FBI's Oklahoma City field office, FBI Criminal Division, U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), U.S. Capitol Police and Oklahoma City Police Department participated in the investigation, the federal law enforcement source said. FBI PROBES SUSPICIOUS WHITE POWDER LETTERS SENT TO SCHUMER, DEM SENATORS AS THREAT SPREADS NATIONWIDE The complaint alleges the mailings date back to September 2024, when state election officials began reporting letters containing a white powdery substance. Investigators identified similar mailings addressed to election officials in all 50 states, 49 of which were either recovered from recipients or intercepted in the mail stream. The initial 2024 mailings contained white powder and a three-page letter titled "DECLARATION OF WAR." The writer threatened that if certain demands were not met, another mailing would be sent to "1000's of destinations" and "it won't be flour next time," according to the complaint. "The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election," the complaint states. ILLINOIS MAN ACCUSED OF THREATENING CONGRESS WITH WHITE SUBSTANCES IN LETTERS MARKED WITH HIS RETURN ADDRESS Testing found the powders examined so far were nonhazardous substances, including yeast or flour, though not every letter has been fully tested, according to the FBI. Investigators said some letters contained hidden messages visible under ultraviolet light. One warned recipients to remain on the "right side of history" and suggested their lives could depend on it. Some mailings listed "U.S.T.E.A.," described as the "United States Traitor Elimination Army," as the sender and gave a return address in Takoma Park, Maryland, according to the complaint. The FBI said surveillance footage showed a vehicle associated with Martin stopping at Postal Service mailboxes in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio in October. Investigators also said Martin's fingerprints were found on a letter sent to FBI Director Kash Patel. Authorities further linked Martin to Walmart purchases of turmeric and vinegar, items investigators said could be used to create writing visible under ultraviolet light. The arrest follows a nationwide investigation into suspicious mail sent to congressional and election offices ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. JUDGE TOSSES CASE AGAINST EX-FBI OFFICIALS ACCUSED OF LYING TO CONGRESS ABOUT HUNTER BIDEN INVESTIGATION The FBI said last month it was working with USPIS to investigate "a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices," The Associated Press reported last month. Authorities warned recipients to treat the mailings as "potentially hazardous" while investigators worked to intercept additional letters before they reached their destinations. The FBI said in an Oct. 23 advisory that no hazardous material had been identified in the suspicious substances tested at that point, though laboratory testing remained ongoing. Several Senate offices reported receiving or being sent suspicious mail. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: A lot of people are ‘feeling betrayed’ by Stevens’s reversal: Jaime Harrison

articles.body:
Former Democratic National Committee Chair Jaime Harrison said people are “feeling betrayed” by Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) last-minute decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race.

“I believe when you give your word, you keep it,” Harrison said during an appearance on The Hill’s broadcasting partner NewsNation. “I think there are a lot of folks who are feeling betrayed because Haley committed to supporting Abdul, and now she’s reneged on that commitment.”

Stevens endorsed Rogers on Sunday following an appearance at a Detroit church event. Her decision comes after a public feud with El-Sayed stemming from a political advertisement.

The ad tied Israel to high grocery prices in the U.S., which resulted in Stevens releasing a statement saying El-Sayed did not condemn the ad forcefully enough.

The two Democrats were initially scheduled to appear at an event on Sunday in Detroit alongside Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.), but El-Sayed asked his former primary opponent to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from Sunday’s event.

In a statement posted to the social platform X on Monday, Stevens defended her decision to back Rogers, saying, “once I concluded that Abdul El-Sayed is not fit to serve in the United States Senate, I had to confront who should.”

“I chose Mike Rogers, with the hope that he can serve in the tradition of John McCain: a senator willing to put country before party and stand up to his own side when conscience requires it,” she added.

Following Stevens’s switch, El-Sayed told reporters , “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

During his NewsNation appearance, Harrison said, “You don’t have to agree with every position a nominee takes, but commitment should mean something.”

Former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel, who was also part of the NewsNation interview, said she thinks the Michigan Senate race might be won by Republicans but could not say the same for Texas or Kansas.

“I think we keep the Senate,” she said. “I think we keep Ohio. I think we win Michigan.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ says El-Sayed is likely to win the Senate race.

articles.title: Russia is maneuvering for the first shots of a space war
articles.summary: The next war may not begin with missiles crossing borders, but with satellites stalking one another in orbit,
articles.body:
A Russian military satellite dangerously maneuvered to follow a vital U.S. orbital radar last month in what seems to be the first use of an in-orbit weapon in space.

Russia’s Cosmos 2612 satellite was observed “stalking” a U.S. registered synthetic aperture radar satellite providing intelligence to Ukraine, positioning it for potential close proximity operations to be used as an orbital weapon.

Commercial space situational awareness data shows a set of six Russian satellites launched in April executing high-energy stalking maneuvers to approach American reconnaissance satellites. These maneuvers cost the Russian satellites a considerable amount of fuel but put them into position to rapidly attack American assets.

“Russia was deploying a space weapon there,” General Stephen Whitting of the U.S. Space Command told the Center for Strategic and International Studies , adding that it was put “into an orbit where they can reach critical U.S. national security satellites.”

This is hugely dangerous, as it is occurring at the same time that Russia seems to be preparing a series of ground-side sabotage operations against NATO allies such as Poland . Russia may be emboldened, as it launched a series of limited gray-zone sabotage operations against Germany in September which resulted in virtually no consequences beyond Berlin ordering the closure of a Russian consulate and cultural center.

Such a muted response signals to Moscow that risks are low, potentially causing it to expand the envelope with space-based gray-zone operations like Cosmos 2612. In short, Cosmos 2612’s trajectory represents a concrete test of Western resolve in space; if it transitions from positioning to action, it could mark the opening shots of more overt orbital conflict.

America should publicly warn Russia now that hostile action against our satellites will be treated as an attack on U.S. interests, with consequences so Moscow knows the price of such irresponsible behavior. Publicly declaring high-value U.S. commercial satellites supporting partners like Ukraine are within America’s defense perimeter would go a long way. Deciding and publicly communicating this now would prevent further Russian gray-zone actions that put humanity’s future in space at immense risk.

The potential consequences of even a limited conflict in space could be devastating. By moving so close to U.S. satellites, Russia risks triggering what scientists call the Kessler syndrome , in which each collision generates space debris that increases the likelihood of further collisions. Thus, any conflict in orbit could quickly get out of hand and jeopardize mankind’s ability to safely access space for multiple generations.

Destroying a satellite in orbit could be the equivalent of firing a shotgun in a crowded room where anyone hit by the initial blast would also be forced to let off a shotgun blast of their own in a dangerous chain reaction. Such a reaction would deprive Russia of its own satellites, but Putin may regard that as a win because the American military is more reliant on space as a force multiplier than Russia.

Roughly 66 percent of active satellites in orbit today belong to SpaceX’s Starlink internet network, which offered the Ukrainian forces fighting Russia such an immense advantage that Putin’s army first tried to adopt it and then began launching sabotage attacks against its ground facilities.

For example, America’s incredible F-35 fighter relies heavily on space-based communications satellites to create the network centric warfare effects that make it such a powerful tool. The satellites that are now vulnerable to Russia are the same ones ensuring that America’s precision weapons can pinpoint targets so accurately that strike errors are measured in inches.

Presently, the U.S. Space Force, the National Reconnaissance Office, and associated assets under U.S. Space Command dominated space and that superiority played a pivotal role in the success of the early strikes against Iran.

At the start of the war, Space Command “ disrupted, degraded, and blinded ” Iran, rendering it vulnerable to incoming threats, preventing early detection or coordinated retaliation as electronic warfare satellites jammed radar systems, interrupted command-and-control networks and scrambled drone and missile-guidance signals.

The current network of large U.S. military and intelligence satellites does provide a major war-winning advantage over other countries, but it was built to operate in an uncontested environment. It simply isn’t resilient to the kind of threat Russia presents.

In 2021 , a Russian anti-satellite weapon forced American astronauts on the International Space Station into the space equivalent of hiding in a bunker, showing just how disturbingly vulnerable the U.S. is in space.

The weapon, a direct-ascent anti-satellite missile, was launched with no warning to America and struck an old satellite during a demonstration. The impact created a massive debris field of more than 1,500 pieces, any of which could do devastating damage to the orbital infrastructure upon which the American military depends.

The next war may not begin with missiles crossing borders, but with satellites stalking one another in orbit, and Americans should be paying attention as that threat comes closer to becoming a reality.

Andrew Follett conducts research analysis for a nonprofit in the Washington area.

articles.body:
South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews made one of her final pitches to voters ahead of Election Day , accusing Sen. Darline Graham (R) of reading from a script written by national Republicans.

“My opponent Darline Graham has been hard to find on the campaign trail,” Andrews told NewsNation’s Leland Vittert late Monday. “When we do hear from her, all she’s doing is reading scripts that were written for her by the same Washington, D.C., insiders and party bosses that handpicked her to be in this seat.”

Graham was appointed to the seat by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) after the death of her brother , the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R). Darline Graham pulled off a close primary win with President Trump’s endorsement but has found herself in an unusually competitive race against Andrews in a state Trump won by nearly 20 points in 2024.

To find success as a Democrat in the Palmetto State, Andrews will have to win over Republicans who are disaffected with their party. She pointed to her support from some within the GOP, including former Gov. David Beasley, who endorsed the Democrat alongside his onetime rival, former Gov. Jim Hodges (D).

“We’ve been building a campaign that’s for everyone, and I think a great symbol of the unity that my campaign represents is my co-endorsement from [Beasley and Hodges],” Andrews said. “We’re bringing people from across the aisle together because I’m willing to put South Carolina first.”

She will also need good turnout from Democrats at the polls. Black voters, who heavily lean Democratic , turned out in strong numbers across the South during the early voting period.

Andrews said the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which significantly weakened the 1965 Voting Rights Act, was a motivating factor for the key voting bloc.

“This reflects what I’m hearing from folks when I go from Black church to Black church,” she told the “On Balance” host. “People are fired up, and they understand that Washington isn’t working for them anymore. … That’s the frustration that’s turning into motivation.”

Still, Democrats have had hope of winning a Senate seat against a Graham in the past.

In 2020, Democrat Jaime Harrison — the former chair of the Democratic National Committee — was neck and neck in polls with Lindsey Graham but ultimately lost by 10 points.

Both parties appear to consider the race competitive this time around, with Republicans spending millions to boost Darline Graham in the final weeks. Nearly all of the GOP candidate’s fundraising has come from outside spending, while most of Andrews’s cash was raised by her campaign.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Graham a 61 percent chance of winning a full term in the upper chamber of Congress.

articles.title: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.summary: At least 38 people are killed in 24 hours and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky warns dozens more could be trapped under rubble.
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Ukraine – including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital – have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.

At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.

He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".

Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.

The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.

Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.

Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof collapsed, trapping many underneath.

"The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.

Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen.

However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.

The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment.

According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital.

But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law" .

Further north, in Dnipro, nearly 50 terminally ill patients were being transferred to other facilities after their hospice was destroyed by a Russian missile on Monday night. The oldest of the patients was 90 years old.

Mayor Boris Filatov posted photos on Telegram showing elderly people lying in their beds in a hospice room with blown-out windows and rubble and broken glass strewn on the floors.

"I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad.

"These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."

Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.

Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating.

The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".

As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.

It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.

Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.

Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.

US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting.

The UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities.

At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.

In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

articles.title: Boebert on whether Johnson should remain as GOP leader after midterms: ‘We’ll see what things look like’

Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) stopped short of committing to support Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) as the top House Republican after Tuesday’s midterm elections, suggesting his future in leadership could depend on the party’s performance at the polls. articles.body:
Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) stopped short of committing to support Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) as the top House Republican after Tuesday’s midterm elections, suggesting his future in leadership could depend on the party’s performance at the polls.

In an interview on Monday with NewsNation’s “The Hill,” Boebert weighed in on whether she wanted Johnson to remain the party’s leader regardless of whether the GOP retained control of the House.

“Look, if the leader of our party brings home victories, then he has every right to be there and lead once again,” Boebert told NewsNation’s Blake Burman. “You don’t fire your coach who takes you to the Super Bowl and wins.”

“Mike Johnson and I talk on a regular basis, and we’ll see what things look like after the midterms,” she continued.

Republicans are facing difficult political terrain heading into Election Day, with control of the House hanging in the balance and Johnson’s future as Speaker potentially riding on the outcome.

Johnson has spent the election cycle working to defend the GOP’s narrow House majority, which has repeatedly complicated Republicans’ efforts to advance President Trump’s legislative agenda.

The top House Republican has made it clear that he has no intentions of giving up his leadership role regardless of the election’s outcome, despite most House Speakers in recent years stepping down after losing the gavel.

Boebert, a staunch Trump ally who has occasionally clashed with Republican leadership, acknowledged that Democrats have an advantage heading into Tuesday’s elections but expressed confidence in her own reelection prospects in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.

“Democrats are definitely motivated,” she said, pointing to Democratic spending and organizing efforts in Colorado. “I do feel comfortable in my seat.”

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted her race from “solid red” to “likely red” in the final weeks of the race in what would ordinarily be a noncompetitive pickup for Republicans. Trump carried the district in 2024 by 18 percentage points, while Boebert secured more than 53 percent of the vote that same year.

articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) last-minute decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed could end up helping the Democratic Senate nominee.

“I have no idea what her thinking was … but I don‘t think it‘s going to have much impact. In fact, if it has any impact, I think it will end up helping Abdul,” Clinton said during an appearance on CNN.

On Sunday, Stevens, who previously backed her former primary opponent, endorsed Rogers following an appearance at a Detroit church event. Her decision came after a public feud with El-Sayed in the preceding days that stemmed from a political advertisement tying Israel to high grocery prices in the U.S.

Stevens released a statement saying El-Sayed did not condemn the ad forcefully enough.

El-Sayed and Stevens were initially scheduled to make a joint appearance at an event on Sunday in Detroit alongside Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.), but El-Sayed asked her to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her. On Sunday, Stevens appeared at church alongside Rogers instead.

Following her decision to reverse her support for El-Sayed, Stevens received backlash from Democrats .

In a statement posted to the social platform X on Monday, Stevens said she chose Rogers “with the hope that he can serve in the tradition of John McCain: a senator willing to put country before party and stand up to his own side when conscience requires it.”

El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’s switch, telling reporters , “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

The Senate race in Michigan has grown competitive, with nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ saying El-Sayed is “likely to win” the race. Nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report also shifted its rating of the race from toss-up to “lean Democrat.”

articles.title: AOC campaign memo frames growth from progressive firebrand to national Democratic Party force
articles.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's campaign memo reveals how she built a nationwide movement around economic populism after Trump's 2024 election victory.
articles.body: An internal strategy memo released by the campaign committee for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N. Y.) and distributed to key allies makes the case that the lawmaker has evolved from a progressive firebrand into a formidable national political force. The five-page document makes no mention of a potential 2028 presidential or Senate run. Instead, it urges stakeholders to view her record as that of one of the Democratic Party's most effective messengers for working-class voters. Following President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory, the memo states, Ocasio-Cortez launched an aggressive nationwide push to rebuild the party around economic populism and establish a broad movement for working families. CARVILLE TORCHES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS AS 'PACK OF FOOLS,' PRAISES AOC'S POLITICAL EVOLUTION "Over the past two years, Rep. Ocasio-Cortez has built a record of success that extends beyond her own electoral victories," the memo reads. "The Congresswoman has emerged as one of the most powerful endorsements in the United States and New York State specifically. Candidates from rural districts and battleground seats see her as an asset for their general election campaigns." The document highlights her fundraising reach, citing more than 2 million contributions totaling $38 million, an average donation of $17. 56, and over $3 million funneled to other Democratic candidates and state parties. 'SQUAD' RAKES IN RECORD $2.35M WHILE SLAMMING THE DOOR ON COP DONATIONS Her small fundraising operation is unmatched in the House and rivals that of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., the memo claims. According to the document, Ocasio-Cortez’s strategy was shaped by post-2024 conversations with "Trump-AOC" split-ticket voters in her New York district, who expressed deep, cross-partisan frustration with a political establishment perceived as favoring corporate billionaires over ordinary workers. BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP "As Democrats tried to understand why Trump had won again, Rep. Ocasio-Cortez argued that the path for the party to win back working class voters should be centered on economic populism, confronting concentrated wealth and power, and revitalizing American democracy," the memo states. The memo points to race-altering endorsements in key primary and general election races across California, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Montana. It highlights Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan and Sam Forstag’s Congressional primary victory in Montana as central case studies of her influence in rural and conservative-leaning areas. AOC SIDES WITH BERNIE-BACKED PROGRESSIVE IN SENATE PRIMARY CLASH WITH SCHUMER ESTABLISHMENT Forstag trailed significantly in the polls before joining Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders on stage at their "Fighting Oligarchy" rally in Missoula, Montana. Following her endorsement and appearance, he was able to erase the deficit and win the Democratic primary. The document outlines a turning point following her unsuccessful bid for ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, alongside a March 2025 budget standoff in which Senate Democratic leadership accepted concessions during federal shutdown negotiations. In response, Ocasio-Cortez shifted focus to taking her message directly to voters. BERNIE SANDERS DISMISSES HALEY STEVENS, SAYS MICHIGAN RACE IS AGAINST THE 'BILLIONAIRE CLASS' Speaking at a rally in Idaho, Ocasio-Cortez laid out the central thesis of her national tour: "I want us all to understand that this constant pressure we feel in our lives—of the water rising up to our throats, the impossibility to afford anything easily, the fear of speaking up or being who we are in public, the bitter divisions driven more by online algorithms than the truth, the crumbling of our rights and protections— understand that this, right now, is what it feels like to be governed by billionaires," she said. In the two years since, the memo states, Ocasio-Cortez has held large-scale rallies in purple, red, and blue places alike. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "She made race-changing endorsements in swing districts and deep-blue party primaries, as well as in her home base of New York City," the memo added.

articles.title: Ten years later, 'Pokémon Go to the polls' still haunts the internet | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Hillary Clinton's 2016 political gaffe has become an irony-shrouded rallying cry for jaded young voters who still dare to hope for change.
articles.body:
In the lead-up to a presidential election that would irrefutably transform American culture, Hillary Clinton took the stage at a rally in Virginia as she campaigned to become the first female president.

“We’re going to have a lot of jobs — jobs from building infrastructure to coding. Creating new apps,” she said. “I don’t know who created Pokémon GO, but I’m trying to figure out how we get them to have Pokémon Go to the polls .”

Ten years later, it is once again Election Day in the United States. Now, most app developers aren’t even writing their own code anymore, thanks to AI, and Pokémon GO has been sold to a company wholly owned by Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. The only thing about that political moment that hasn’t changed is that “Pokémon Go to the polls” memes still crop up on every Election Day.

“It was very bold and confident, and also just sounded so terribly out of touch and corny,” Cesar Ruiz de Castilla, an elected ward committee member in Philadelphia, told TechCrunch. “I don’t know if the mainstream media cared that much about it, but everyone was making a meme about it and talking about it online.”

Since then, digital culture has become increasingly inextricable from the fate of American politics. Donald Trump tweeted his way through his first term, then later started his own social media platform ; presidential campaigns hire meme managers ; the White House invites podcasters and content creators to press briefings; Elon Musk even spun up his own advisory group under Trump that named itself after the cutesy doge meme and then slashed international aid programs.

“The 2016 election was such a monumental moment in internet history, and we were all there for it — our politics have become more, not just divided, but segmented online,” Organizer Memes , a political influencer who teaches Gen Z activists how to reach their peers online via memes, told TechCrunch. “It’s a relic of an optimistic, bygone political era.”

Now, people who weren’t even old enough to vote in 2016 reflect on the year as a cultural turning point, even calling it “ the last good year .” It’s a sentiment that isn’t so much political as it is rooted in nostalgia for an era of internet culture before AI slop, when we used social media to connect with friends, rather than doomscrolling through an algorithmic feed of people we don’t even follow.

At the start of the new year, this yearning for the old internet became a viral sentiment as millions of people shared throwback photos from 2016 on Instagram.

Spotify reported that user-generated playlists featuring 2016 in their titles spiked 790% in the first three weeks of the year, and the company changed its Instagram bio at the time to say it’s “romanticizing 2016 again.”

Never mind that, at the time, the internet perceived 2016 as a cursed year, even before the election — months earlier, one Slate columnist wondered how 2016 compared to 1348, the year the Black Death took hold in Europe.

“[Pokémon Go to the polls] is in that era of the singular internet, when Facebook and Twitter and Tumblr were all kind of bouncing content back-and-forth and not just this complete anarchic mess of 25 platforms that we now have and don’t use,” Organizer Memes said.

Organizer Memes also notes that some cultural touchstones that felt more significant then — like the obsession with Harambe the gorilla — haven’t had as much staying power as “Pokémon Go to the polls.”

Perhaps this is because we’re bound to remember “Pokémon Go to the polls” every few years on Election Day, and because it appeals to both sides of the aisle. On the right, it’s a way to make fun of Democrats, and on the left, it’s a shared groan of embarrassment.

“It’s like if all the kids in a class are making a joke, and then the teacher gets in on the joke, and it stops being funny,” Mack Finkel, who canvassed at the polls on Tuesday on behalf of a healthcare workers’ union, told TechCrunch. “I think there’s a key essence of millennial cringe happening here, and it’s the same reason that all my friends are rewatching [HBO’s] ‘Girls.’”

Clinton’s decade-old, corny comment can be seen as a precursor to the “ Kamala is brat ” meme. While the former vice president’s record as a prosecutor initially made her unpopular among some left-leaning young voters, they rallied around her once she became the only alternative to Trump. Gen Z rallied around Harris by creating flashy, absurdist “fan cam”-style edits of the candidate’s best quips in the aesthetic of Charli XCX’s album “Brat,” which soundtracked the summer of 2024.

“Previously the views I saw about Harris were making fun of her being a cop, like her history as attorney general in California with truancy laws ,” Jess Rauchberg, an assistant professor of communications at the University of Leeds, told TechCrunch at the time . “Now we see that same style of memeification, but it’s an endorsement.”

It’s hard to say why “Pokémon Go to the polls” jokes still make us laugh — whether we’re mocking Clinton or expressing solidarity with others who keep showing up to vote, even as each passing year leaves us feeling more cynical.

“Pokémon Go to the polls” is a way of urging others to make the time to vote and take Election Day seriously, while still acknowledging disappointment with aging lawmakers who don’t know what it’s like to come of age in the social media era. It’s shrouded in enough irony to project a sense of jaded detachment, yet remains a desperate, earnest plea to our friends: Please, just go vote.

articles.title: Michigan US Senate race: Rogers, El-Sayed urge turnout for critical race
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed hopes to become the first Muslim US senator as Michigan’s Senate race reaches its critical final hours.
articles.body:
Michigan voters are casting their ballots in a charged, closely watched race that could make Democrat Abdul El-Sayed the first Muslim in the United States Senate and help decide control of the chamber.

Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, cast his ballot at a polling station in White Lake, Michigan hours after polls opened. El-Sayed had already had his vote submitted and counted through an absentee ballot before Election Day.

The two candidates seek to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. A final New York Times/Siena poll placed El-Sayed 11 points ahead of Rogers going into the election.

Polls opened at 7am local time (12:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday). If the race is close, it may not be called until later on Wednesday. The US Department of Justice has announced that election monitors will be present at the polls in Michigan and all 50 other states, a first in US history.

El-Sayed, a Muslim born to Egyptian parents, is the former head of Detroit’s health department and has campaigned on progressive policies such as Medicare for All.

Rogers, a former congressman and close ally of US President Donald Trump, is seeking to come back after a narrow loss to a Democrat in a 2024 Senate race.

Democrats need to gain four seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections to wrest back the Senate from Republicans and rein in Trump. The race is also seen as a test of whether a progressive who openly criticises Israel can win in a swing state.

Both candidates made a final push on social media as voting got under way.

“It’s time. It’s up to us to show the country what’s possible. The world is watching,” El-Sayed wrote, sharing an upbeat campaign video that features former US President Barack Obama.

Rogers posted a video that featured interviews with supporters, one of whom called El-Sayed an “extremist”.

“We have a state to save”, the post read.

Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer gave a firm endorsement of El-Sayed after casting his own ballot in New York’s race.

“There are millions of Michiganders whose number one issue is getting their costs down,” said Schumer.

“Abdul El-Sayed is … talking to the people about those issues and doing things about them … He is going to win tonight because he’s talking about what Michiganders care about.”

The El-Sayed campaign’s final days were overshadowed by a rift with Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a fellow Democrat whom El-Sayed narrowly defeated in a primary election in August.

On Sunday, Stevens endorsed Rogers , saying she was “choosing country over hate” and capping off a weeks-long row about El-Sayed’s opposition to US support for Israel.

Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, and the pro-Israel lobbying group the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent more than $30m backing her against El-Sayed. A majority of her large donors lined up to support Rogers after her loss, channeling $9m into a Republican group that supports him, according to The New York Times.

El-Sayed, by contrast, has accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and argued that US aid to Israel would be better spent at home.

Asked by NewsNation on her way in to vote for Rogers whether her change in support was worth it, Stevens replied: “Absolutely. Voting is always worth it, right?”

Senate leader Schumer, who had initially backed Stevens, was asked whether her defection could hand the election to Republicans. “Haley Stevens is one vote,” he replied.

El-Sayed, the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrants, has faced persistent attacks on his faith. Republican Party ads have sought to link him to “terrorism” and radicalism, with Trump joining in the inflammatory rhetoric.

The US president has repeatedly called El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a “nasty guy”, mocking his name and repeating an unfounded, widely circulated Republican claim that he belongs to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Hours before polls opened, Trump once again took aim at El-Sayed, this time in a post on his Truth Social platform.

“Abdul El-Sayed Hates Jews and Hates Blacks. Don’t feel bad, he also Hates Whites. Only fools would vote for him in the Michigan race for the U.S. Senate! He will, 100%, do you in! VOTE FOR MIKE ROGERS,” Trump wrote.

The US president also mentioned El-Sayed in a Fox News interview early on Election Day, when he said annual US financial aid to Israel should stop at the end of 2026.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they [Israel] don’t need it?” he said.

articles.title: Republicans fight to hold on to the Senate as Democrats seek gains in traditionally red states
articles.summary: Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal and alleged ballot shenanigans.
articles.body: Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal, alleged ballot shenanigans and President Donald Trump’s incessant swooning over the backside of one Republican candidate. Close races are expected in several traditional battlegrounds — including Georgia, Michigan and North Carolina — but also in states that have become more reliably red since Trump’s rise in politics, such as Ohio and Iowa. There also are closer-than-expected races brewing in even redder states such as Alaska, Kansas and Texas. Underscoring the high stakes: More than $3.4 billion has been spent on television and digital advertisements in Senate races across the country, according to tracking firm AdImpact. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber, meaning Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to regain control. Follow live election coverage here. The consequences for Trump are significant. For the past two years, his own Republican Party has controlled both chambers of Congress, allowing him to pursue his agenda largely unchecked. But if the Republicans lose the Senate, he’ll need Democratic cooperation to move forward on legislation and appointments. Democrats will have increased power to pursue investigations into the administration. Alaska has emerged late as a closely watched contest. Democrat Mary Peltola is under scrutiny after a New York Times report that her campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate into the race — Dan J. Sullivan — with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The “ballot-stacking” tactic is seen as a way to sow confusion among voters in a state that uses ranked choice voting and has four Senate candidates on the ballot. Peltola and her campaign have repeatedly denied allegations that they recruited the lesser-known Sullivan. Polls close in Alaska at 1 a.m. ET. Clarity about the fight for the Senate will come much earlier in states such as Ohio, where polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET, and Michigan, where the last polls close at 9 p.m. ET. In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted faces a tough challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the race to serve the remaining two years on JD Vance’s unexpired Senate term. Husted was appointed to fill the seat temporarily last year after Vance was elected vice president. Polls have shown a close race in Ohio, and the president held three rallies in the state in recent weeks — as well as one in the Cincinnati media market, in neighboring Kentucky — in an effort to boost Husted. Trump used the rallies not only to promote Husted’s work as a senator, but also to compliment his physique. Trump, who often gives the impression that he is casting for a movie, repeatedly praised Husted’s “ass” in Ohio and elsewhere down the stretch. “If Husted wins,” one senior Republican official told NBC News last week, “it’s because Trump literally dragged his ass over the finish line.” Then there’s the Michigan race, which is ending on an explosive note. The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, scored a surprise last-minute endorsement Sunday from Rep. Haley Stevens, who in August lost the Democratic nomination to challenge him. Stevens had vowed as late as Saturday, publicly and privately, to not break her promise to vote for Abdul El-Sayed. The Democrats had long clashed over his criticism of Israel, but Stevens’ criticism had intensified in recent days, prompting the El-Sayed campaign to signal that she was no longer welcome at his events. Stevens cited that in her decision to defect to Rogers, sparking outrage and accusations of betrayal from House Democratic colleagues. Other key races to watch Tuesday include Maine, where polls close at 8 p.m., and where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is up against Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson. And at 9 p.m. ET, the last polls will close in Texas, which hasn’t had a Democratic senator in 33 years. The race took on a heightened energy after the Republican incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, lost a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after a heavy push by Trump in favor of the latter. Democrats are excited about their candidate, state Rep. James Talarico, who has maintained steady leads in polls, though within the margin of error. Trump ally and tech billionaire Elon Musk, meanwhile, has spent at least $150 million to back Paxton.

House Democrats are hoping they'll get good news on election night, but they're still tamping down some of the rosiest projections about their performance.

"A good night looks like taking back the House. That's step one. Building a larger majority is step two," said House Majority PAC spokesperson CJ Warnke, adding that a Democratic majority between 225 and 230 seats might be most realistic.

Democrats have had to compete on redder turf even before this cycle's redistricting; this Congress, only three Republicans held seats won by Kamala Harris, while many more Democrats were in Trump-won districts.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats are watching seats in Indiana, Kentucky, Virginia, and Florida that have been on the outside of the House battlefield. Strong performances there could indicate a blue tsunami. And the more seats they gain, the more manageable Hakeem Jeffries' governing coalition would become next year.

articles.title: Ballot scanners glitch in N.Y., officials say ballots are safe
articles.summary: Voting machines in polling sites in Westchester County, N.Y., had glitches Tuesday when the ballot scanners stopped accepting votes, officials said.
articles.body:
Nov. 3 (UPI) -- Voting machines at polling sites in Westchester County, N.Y., had glitches Tuesday when the ballot scanners stopped accepting votes, state officials reported.

New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, said voters can still safely vote at their usual precincts.

"My office is monitoring this issue with scanners in Westchester and is in touch with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a solution," James posted on X . "Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count."

The issues began when the polls opened at 6 a.m., Westchester County executive Ken Jenkins told The Hill.

"While technical issues can be frustrating, contingency procedures exist for precisely these circumstances," Kathleen R. McGrath, a spokesperson for the New York State Board of Elections, said in a statement . "Bipartisan election officials are diligently working to ensure every eligible voter has the opportunity to cast their ballot."

The county's board of elections said the exact cause of the malfunction is unclear but it affected every ballot scanner in the county.

"The Westchester Board of Elections wants to reassure every voter that your vote matters, your ballot will be secure, and your vote will be counted," the board said.

Voters should continue to fill out their paper ballots, which will be placed into orange emergency ballot bags, secured and counted later.

Minor issues with voting machines are not uncommon.

"Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted," the state board said in a statement.

Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., who represents the area, reminded people to stay and vote.

"We do not yet know the exact cause of the issue, whether it is the ballot or the machine. The Board of Elections is working with their vendors to resolve it," Lawler said. "However, every ballot will be counted. Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting."

Lawler's competitive opponent Cait Conley also told voters on X to cast their votes.

"Don't worry: you can still vote and every vote is being counted! Don't be dissuaded and have your voice heard. The issue is being worked on diligently by the Board of Elections in a bipartisan manner. The Polls are open and operational, and every vote cast will be counted. Please stay in line and have your voice heard as they work to resolve the issue."

Derek Tisler, a lawyer with the Brennan Center who specializes in election administration and security, told The New York Times that while the situation in Westchester County appeared to be more widespread than typical glitches, it was still "well within the world of possibilities that election officials plan for."

As word of the glitch made the rounds, conspiracy theorists began spreading unfounded claims.

Posts mentioning the words "cheat," "steal," "rig" and the like boosted to more than 100 per minute in the earlier part of the day, according to analysis of data from TweetBinder by Audisense, The New York Times reported .

"In some places, these real issues -- and the proposed remedies -- are getting picked up with conspiratorial framing that falsely suggests that the malfunctions are intentional," Kate Starbird, a disinformation researcher and co-founder of the University of Washington's Center for an Informed Public, posted on on Bluesky .

"No surprise," said Claudia Tenney, Republican representative for New York's 24th Congressional District, posted on X . "The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat."

But Westchester County is a heavily Democratic district, and errors in voting are more likely to help Republicans in that area, The Times reported.

Broward County, Fla., also had glitches in voting machines Tuesday morning. Local media reported that some voters were turned away. Broward is also a Democratic-leaning county.

New York's polling stations are open until 9 p.m. EST.

articles.body: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter. And welcome to election night. NBC News’ “Decision ’26” coverage has begun, and we’ll have 13 hours of continuous live coverage. More than a dozen of our journalists will be bringing you the latest from battlegrounds across the country. Let’s get into it. NBC News has been crisscrossing the United States for months, taking the temperature of voters and campaigns in today’s crucial fight for control of Congress. Senior national politics reporter Jonathan Allen even took a nearly 1,000-mile road trip for a six-day, eight-stop look at Americans’ concerns along Interstate 80.
